{"translation_en":"CHRISTIAN:\n  **I love you** so much.","larger_context_summary":"During the courtship sequence associated with the balcony scene, Christian addresses Roxane, who believes him to be the eloquent author of the letters that have deepened her love. Christian tries to woo her without Cyrano’s verbal assistance but can produce only plain declarations, which Roxane finds emotionally and rhetorically inadequate. The immediate stakes are both romantic and deceptive: Christian wants to sustain Roxane’s affection, while Cyrano’s hidden authorship and his own unspoken love for her complicate the encounter. Cyrano will take over the wooing through the darkness, speaking with the eloquence Roxane expects from Christian.","interpretive_commentary":"The line is primarily a truth-evaluable avowal: Christian presents his love as a fact about his present emotional state. “So much” raises the stated degree of that love, but intensity is not the same as expressive or reflexive force; in this scene the declaration is deliberate, conventional, and strategically addressed rather than an involuntary outburst. Its courtship setting gives it limited relational significance, since saying it may encourage intimacy and sustain Roxane’s expectations, yet the wording contains no promise, pledge, or explicit undertaking. The broader deception—Roxane attributes Cyrano’s eloquence and letters to Christian—does not erase the line’s core semantic force or necessarily make Christian’s professed feeling false. Dramatically, its importance lies in its inadequacy: Christian’s sincerity-seeming declaration cannot provide the verbal richness Roxane desires."}
